speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government has been notified by the United States Secretary of State that he has declined the request of the government of Canada for the extradition of Hal Banks charged with perjury committed in Ottawa. The ground for the decision of the Secretary of State is that extradition is sought on a charge of perjury arising directly out of the denial of guilt of a non-extradictable offence.
It is the view of the Canadian authorities that this exception does not exist under the terms of the extradition convention between Canada and the United States. In these circumstances the Canadian government is

speechtext: I am sure all hon. member are reading the newspapers very carefully these days and looking at the international financial crisis. One aspect of this international financial crisis is a continuing increase in interest rates, and that is why there is no easy answer to the problem of interest rates. It is a very disturbing aspect of the international financial situation, and until that situation is clarified I do not see much prospect of lower interest rates.

increasing the gold price as one way of meeting the problem of high interest rates?

intention of the Canadian government to take actions that would disturb the international monetary markets more than they are now disturbed. Does the minister not agree that interest rates began rising when United States gold reserves began dropping? Rates have risen in direct proportion to the loss of United States gold reserves.

The greatest contribution would be to bring into operation the supplementary drawing rights, on which we have worked for some time, to supplement the existing gold stocks and facilitate, therefore, international transactions and help to end the sort of financial disturbance that is now prevailing.
Is it not true that for the past 5,000 years of recorded history human beings have been seeking a substitute for gold? So far they have not found one that is universally acceptable.

speechtext:
In the post-war period we found means to supplement gold. The International Monetary Fund was created for the purpose of supplementing gold and providing another means of carrying on international transactions, that is, transactions between countries, and financing them. I believe the

time has come when we ought to carry this process a stage further. No one has suggested that gold ought to be eliminated as a reserve for international purposes. It would be very useful if we had a supplement to gold and we did not need to depend entirely on gold, the price of which could be changed, in order to make our international monetary system function well.

I agree with the minister, and we must use the services of the I.M.F. and various other international bodies. Is it not obvious, though, that what happened in the past can happen again? The present situation seems to be adding a headache to a brain tumor. Measures which are taken seem merely to delay the crisis. They do not cure it. Is it not true that this crisis engulfs the world? I have read a report that about 200 tons of gold will change hands on the London market today. How long can this go on?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot answer that last question. In the post-war period, when we introduced modern, international financial mechanisms, we saw the greatest expansion and prosperity that the world has ever seen. I regret that we now face this sort of international crisis. I suggest, none the less, that this international crisis will not be solved simply. I think the best way of dealing with it would be to carry into effect the new kinds of international reserves that have been under discussion among countries of the world for the past couple of years. I regret that we have not had a sufficient degree of international agreement to bring those reserves into effect. If we could do that I do not think we would be faced with the present crisis.

May I ask the minister one more question? Does the government still intend to supply gold to the United States and to subsidize the United States to the tune of 14 per cent while so doing? We sold to the United States $100 million worth of gold but that gold cost us $114 million to produce because we pay a subsidy to our gold mining companies. [DOT] (3:40 p.m.)

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Our policy has been to keep a certain proportion of our reserves in gold and a certain proportion in other forms of exchange, chiefly American dollars invested in the United States and earning interest. I believe this is the proper policy for Canada. I

believe it is only prudent we should hold part of our reserves in gold as long as the present international financial system operates. I do not believe it would be prudent for Canada to hold all its reserves in gold. We would lose a great deal of revenue if we did so and successive ministers of finance would be obliged to impose still higher taxation in order to meet expenditures. So I think it is very wise to have invested a substantial part of our reserves in interest bearing securities.
Gold earns us nothing. It is sterile. We hold it because under the present international system we want to have some protection against the possibility that at some time in the future the price of gold might be increased. But I do not think it would be in the Canadian interest to keep more than a certain proportion of our reserves in gold. I believe that from time to time we shall sell some of our gold stocks and turn them into something which produces earnings to keep down taxation in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I only have two or three questions for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp).
In view of the confusion now prevailing, both among the Canadian people and the deputation in general, as well as among some teachers in our Quebec schools, because of this mad or panicky gold rush which results in gold transactions between various countries, could the minister now state that, as far as our Canadian currency is concerned, the gold guarantee is no longer of any account since May 1, 1940, but that the Canadian gold reserve, as he just said, is only used for the international transactions which may be effected at a given time, in short, that gold is of no use at all to guarantee the currency in circulation in the country, under our monetary system? Is the minister in a position to tell us that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, what the hon. gentleman has said is right. We retain a gold reserve for the purpose of settling international transactions. As I said in reply to the hon. member for Timmins, we have followed a policy of keeping part gold and part American dollars or dollars invested in United States securities, bearing in mind the fact that the United States dollar is based upon gold and one can never tell whether or not in the future the price of gold might be changed.
March 14, 1968

This has been the policy followed by successive governments over a long period and I think it is prudent. I agree with the hon. gentleman that a Canadian dollar bill cannot be presented in exchange for gold. Gold is retained for use in settling international transactions and for that purpose it is in my view, a very valuable part of our reserves.

Mr. Chairman, my other question is this.
A moment ago, the Minister of Finance, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin), said that Canada had to go along with the current of international affairs and that we must not upset the present course of the unsteady economy.
So one could say that we are only the followers of policies enacted internationally by foreign countries, that we must necessarily suffer the consequences of decisions taken in Washington, France, or England, and that we are unable to set down a clear and definite economic policy.
Now, I would like to ask the minister-I admit that there is now a severe international crisis and that perhaps some heads will roll in a few days or a few weeks-whether there is some law here in Canada which prevents the Canadian government or the Minister of Finance from using strictly Canadian, national credits, in order to ease the situation, and to boost the economy of the country again independently of other countries? Do we not have the means to implement something in this country without always having to run to the United States, to England, to Russia, or to other countries in the world?
At this point, I should like to put this question to the hon. Minister of Finance: Is there an act which prevents the government or the Department of Finance from using the services of the Bank of Canada to create new, debt-free, interest-free credit, a step which would not only have no influence on the international market, but, on the contrary, would enable us to increase our productivity, and would enable us to compete better than at the present time?
Does the hon. minister have any objection to using strictly national credit for Canadians, to boost the Canadian economy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In so far as transactions within Canada are concerned, this is exactly what
Income Tax Act
we do. We have established a credit system, a very complicated and very delicate financial mechanism comprised of many kinds of institutions under the control of the monetary policy of the country through the Bank of Canada. But when it comes to international transactions then, of course, it is necessary to have something which foreigners want and will accept, and there are only two things I should like to have in my reserve in this situation. One of them is gold, which will be accepted by anyone, and the second is United States dollars which remain the most acceptable currency in the world and the currency in which we must settle most of our international transactions. We do have provisions for satisfying our internal credit needs and while we make use of them in a way which may not be altogether to the liking of the hon. member, the system works very well on the whole. But it will not work internationally.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. minister has just told us that he does not necessarily share the political ideas the Ralliement Creditiste advocates, but did the right hon. Prime Minister not tell us Tuesday in his speech that the government had only two ways of managing the country or making expenditures: borrow money or levy taxes?
Well, Mr. Chairman, the hon. Minister of Finance knows full well that there is another way. If the government is sovereign, could the minister not resort to the credit of the Bank of Canada to balance Canada's economy on the basis of Canadian production. Why does the department not use the Bank of Canada to create the credit matching that production?
What prevents it from doing that? The law?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have had many discussions across the floor on this subject with the hon. gentleman as well as with other members of his party and those associated with him such as the hon. member for Lapointe. I do not think we are going to agree this afternoon on the best way of accomplishing our respective purposes. The government has responsibility for monetary policy and the Bank of Canada is the agency that is used to implement that policy. The Bank of Canada controls the volume of money in Canada, the volume of dollars that are created for the

March 14, 1968
Income Tax Act
purpose of facilitating the financial system. The money that is put into circulation by the Bank of Canada becomes the foundation upon which other institutions extend credit.
The hon. gentleman is very well aware of the process, and so am I. We may differ as to how it actually works, but at any rate that is the way it is done. I am of the view that the operations of the Bank of Canada, like the operations of the Federal Reserve System in the United States or the Bank of England in England or the Bank of France in France or the Central Bank in Germany, are the accepted, tried and tested methods of controlling the expansion of credit.
I know my hon. friend has a different view. I know I despair of converting him to my view and I hope he despairs of converting me to his point of view, but at any rate I think we understand our respective points of view. I of course have the advantage over him that the point of view I believe is appropriate to the modern world, to our democratic institutions and so on, is accepted throughout the world. I do not believe there is any country in the world that has yet been wise or foolish enough to accept the views of my hon. friend.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to put a final question.
The minister just said that the Bank of Canada determines the volume of credit or money in circulation. Could he tell us who creates this volume and increases it? No doubt the minister is in a position to recognize that the Bank of Canada plays only a minor part in the whole monetary organization in Canada-not fiscal but monetary. In fact, if the federal government issues bonds for $1 billion and the Bank of Canada purchases, to-morrow morning, $1 billion in bonds, the minister is in a position to say that chartered banks have the power, under the law, to multiply that credit by fourteen. It is at that point that the Bank of Canada controls the volume of credit, that is by purchasing from the government a bond which chartered banks have the means to multiply by fourteen and, moreover, to charge interest on the multiplication by fourteen.
I understand that the minister can say that my point of view differs from his, that his point of view is different from mine and that both must be respected. I respect the minister as a man, but on the other hand, I do not respect his point of view which is keeping the country in the economic chaos now

experienced and which is merely due to a financial problem. If the minister stated: "Tomorrow morning, we are going to use the Bank of Canada", the situation would be different. Why does not the Bank of Canada perform that multiplication by fourteen instead of leaving the matter in the hands of a few bankers who are empowered to handle the economic life of the whole country?
If the Bank of Canada multiplied the government commitment by fourteen, that money would be put in circulation interest-free to finance municipalities, provinces, school boards-the government would no longer have to reduce its urgent expenses. We would then see new buildings going up, new industries created, and so on. The wage earners or those who make profits as contractors would deposit these sums in the chartered banks, so that the deposits in the chartered banks would probably be the same as now, but instead of paying interest on the fourteen to one ratio which the chartered banks can apply now, we could have credit free of debt or interest, if you wish, even if we had to repay the amount we have received from the Bank of Canada over a certain period of time and with allowance made for the depreciation of the facilities built.
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance must be able to tell us that the present amount of money, of credit in circulation is in the hands of the chartered banks and not in the hands of the credit unions, even if, as the minister tells us, the Bank of Canada dictates or controls the amount of credit in circulation. I know very well that if I go into a bank tomorrow and borrow $1,000-which I do not have on me since I am borrowing it-if the chartered bank lends me this $1,000, I open a savings account, not a current account. The accounts of other people are not diminished by my opening a savings account while I have no money, but there is $1,000 in my newly-opened account.
As soon as I open a savings account, the chartered bank which lent me the money can use it as reserves deposited in the Bank of Canada and multiply by fourteen the $1,000 it just lent me.
That is where the trouble lies. That is the system which has put us in the situation which the Minister of Finance is now facing. That is the system which is to blame for unemployment in Canada, which forces the Minister of Finance to ask all the other ministers: Cut down your expenses, stop certain
March 14, 1968

Income Tax Act
projects, scrap others, do not encourage production in Canada, lor we do not have the financial means needed.
Mr. Chairman, that is the basis of the difficulty facing the government at the present time. There are, in Canada, at the present time 500,000 unemployed, 80,000 of them in the city of Montreal alone. This includes those who are registered and excludes those who are not. Those who receive social welfare allowances are not considered as unemployed but they are anyway.
At the present time, we ask for the completion of winter works in some places. We are told that we cannot afford it, that we have to reduce our expenses. It is not permitted to carry out certain projects, to build roads, hospitals, buildings which the Canadian people need. By so doing, those who are in need are refused assistance.
Mr. Chairman, why does the hon. Minister of Finance not turn to the Bank of Canada? Why does he simply tell us: The Bank of Canada is at the service of the chartered banks to determine the volume of the money supply? The chartered banks are the ones who decide, not the Bank of Canada. However, I do not know of any law which prevents the hon. Minister of Finance from using the credit of the Bank of Canada.
If the government, this afternoon or tomorrow, would turn to the Bank of Canada to create such credits, that would add immediately to the reserves of the chartered banks and would allow them to increase those reserves 14 times. It would be a repetition of the situation which we have known in 1940, 1941, and 1942 when two Liberal members, Messrs. Arthur Slaght, of Parry Sound, and Gerry McGeer, of Vancouver, asked the Minister of Finance, Mr. Ilsley, who had created, through the Bank of Canada a new credit of $200 millions, I think, in order to finance the first war projects: Why do you not repeat that initiative, in order to finance the Canadian economy? And, Mr. Ilsley, answered: We cannot repeat that indefinitely, because as soon as we use a new credit of the Bank of Canada, it gives the chartered banks the power to multiply their reserves 10, 12, 15 or even 20 times, it puts in their hands an inflationary power. That is the inflationary power held today by the chartered banks. This is exactly the same situation and the hon. Minister of Finance knows it.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
People can laugh about the present situation, but it is not funny. The Canadian people are not willing to face another depression for the sake of the sacrosanct dollar. The Canadian people are not willing to let their natural resources go down the drain to support the financial system.
Mr. Chairman, the Bank of Canada should be used fully to finance the expenditures of the federal government, the provincial governments and the municipal governments.
Speaking of municipalities, we know they are in a slump right now. The Union des municipalites de la province de Quebec is meeting in Quebec these days. I am speaking of the municipalities of the province of Quebec, but the same goes for all the municipalities. They are forced to raise their taxes. The Quebec premier told their representatives: When the provincial budget comes down, we will try to levy new taxes to help you.
We dig one hole to fill another, and the more we do, the larger the hole becomes in the attempt to fill the others.
The situation is the same in Ontario. The government has just approved new taxes on gas, tobacco, parimutuel, all kinds of things and then we are told: That alone will not suffice, we will have to cut expenditures. Ottawa cuts expenditures, Quebec cuts expenditures, and Ontario too. Saskatchewan, under Mr. Thatcher, has also raised its taxes in every field.
Mr. Chairman, how far will the Minister of Finance lead us in that direction? Until we face a depression like the one we had in 1929-30? Is it preferable to plunge 20 million people into an economic depression and to increase the power of the few individuals in Canada who control the economic blood of our country, that is money? For they are the ones who would have us kneel before them when we sit in committee to study the sob stories of the financial community.
Mr. Chairman, it is time, I feel, for the Canadian Minister of Finance and the Canadian government to stand up and tell big finance: Instead of enslaving the people, you will serve the people. This is the trouble today. Instead of serving the people, they enslave the people; instead of bringing financiers to their senses, we obey them.
The Minister of Finance should seriously consider the situation. I understand that he may say we do not share point of view, but I

have been advocating this philosophy for thirty years. When I became a Creditiste, over thirty years ago, I was only 19 or 20 years old. Why did 1 become a Creditiste? Because I never understood how it was that we were left literally to starve during the 1929-39 depression, while billions of dollars were found to wage the 1939-45 war.
How is it that for ten years, our colleges and institutions were only half filled, whereas during the war, there was insufficient space? Industries were sprouting throughout Canada. And now, 20 years after the war, as we must begin to refund what we had borrowed for the slaughter, we are facing facts: we must repay not only the capital, but also the interest. We have managed to pay that interest for the past 25 years. Today, it is the capital which must be paid. We have already paid $20 or $25 billion in interest since the end of the 1939-45 war, and our national debt still reaches $25 billion today. We have not paid a single cent of capital. We have paid, on the average, $1 billion a year in interests only on a fictitious debt created out of nothing by the Canadian banking system.
If the minister and the government had obtained interest-free loans from the Bank of Canada to meet their expenses, we would not find ourselves in such a situation. I challenge the minister to find a proper solution. Even if he doubles the taxes, introduces a bill providing for a 25 or 30 per cent tax increase, he will still not be able to meet his obligations, because the present system is not designed to cope with such a situation. The system is conceived to crush the government and the Canadian nation, and we are not getting rid of it.
Mr. Chairman, I say to the Minister of Finance that he has both the moral and the administrative obligation to put an end to this damnable financial system which oppresses the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words to the minister in this connection. I was surprised to hear the minister talk in the last few days about the international crisis and then brag today about the financial systems of all the nations in the western world. I cannot help but say to him that he has put forward one of the greatest contradictions in respect of finance that I have heard for a long long time. Surely he must understand that the people of Canada,
[Mr. Caouette.l
having considered the situation very carefully, have decided that the present financial system of the government has failed absolutely due to the fact that bank interest rates are now as high as 12J and 13 per cent. If anyone in this or any other country suggests there is a sound reason that interest rates should be as high as 12 or 13 per cent, then all I can say is 1 would have to see much stronger evidence than I have seen to date.
I believe that any alert minister of finance should be very careful to listen at this time to anyone who has anything to offer, whether it be good or bad, and assess what he has to say. Otherwise the minister would be very much like the individual who, when a person to whom he owed some money said "let us cancel the debt", said, "I would rather die owing you than not pay". If the minister continues in this way we will be faced with a situation which no one in this or any other country would like to see.
I should like to refer briefly to a small but powerful book. I suggest the Minister of Finance is quite aware of it. It was written by Vincent Cartwright Vickers. He was deputy lieutenant of the city of London, a director of Vickers Limited for 22 years and a director of London Assurance from which he resigned in January, 1939. In 1910 he was made a governor of the Bank of England and resigned this appointment in 1919. I wish the minister would compare what Mr. Vickers had to say with the situation which has been outlined by the minister over the last couple of weeks. In the opening paragraph on page 1 of this book entitled "Economic Tribulation" Mr. Vickers had this to say:
Slowly but Inevitably the old financial system is crumbling under the weight of modern conditions and the better education of the people; the sooner it crumbles the better, and the sooner it gives way to a better and more modern technique the sooner will the world achieve good will and peace amongst men.
The present order of things must change. The economic structure of civilization is obviously leaning heavily. To build upon it, to add weight to it as it now stands, crooked and unsafe, can only bring nearer the day of its collapse.
Today we are approaching the situation this man had in mind when he said that slowly but surely the mills of the gods would grind. What was written in 1941 by this man who for nine years was governor of the Bank of England we find expressed in the words of the minister today. When the minister says he does not understand what is meant when someone talks about changing the situation to one of an increasing involvement by the Bank
March 14. 1968

of Canada in the debt of our country, I cannot understand to whom he is listening.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The minister said today that we have a fine financial system. Yet we find him also saying that the world is facing a terrible crisis and that the international monetary situation is almost beyond repair. We are now experiencing one of the greatest financial crises we have ever experienced. The situation is almost chaotic. It does seem to me that the time has come when we must stop burying our heads in the sand like ostriches and waving our tail-feathers in the air like palm trees. According to the Minister of Finance that is the position we are to assume.
I do not think the minister listened to what the hon. member for Villeneuve said and I do not think he intends to read what he said when and if he ever has the chance during the campaign. Let me tell the minister that if he expects to become the prime minister of this country and take it upon his shoulders to formulate Canadian policy he had better keep his ears tuned to some of the things which have been said. Let me refer him to the warnings given during the meetings of the committee on finance. He was told that if there was not some control of competition for deposits by trust companies and banks we would find ourselves in a terrible position because of high interest rates. I do not know how anyone can find himself in this position without being very much concerned. When we were discussing the effects of competition for deposits the Governor of the Bank of Canada said he did not anticipate high interest rates for ten years. That was the shortest ten years of my life.

Mr. Chairman, I was very interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Timmins but I do not entirely agree with his contention. I am not sure what the real situation is in respect of gold but I am concerned about what seems to be a lack of interest on the part of the minister in what appears to be a calamity. Canada may not operate on the gold standard but we are tied very closely to the United States which does. The United States now has a national debt of some $64 billion in short and long term paper. In support of this debt the United States has approximately $10 billion in gold. If all the short term money was recalled the United States would be bankrupt.
Canada has reserves to the extent of about one-tenth of those held by the United States.
Income Tax Act
We are tied very closely to their dollar. For many reasons we do not use Canadian dollars in international trade but use United States dollars. If their dollar collapses, even though the minister may not be worried about what will happen to the United States it will bankrupt the Canadian economy. We will then not only be bankrupt like the United States but the Canadian dollar will be at a higher rate and we will lose our trade with every nation in the world. We will be middling rich but starving.
Yesterday about $200 million in gold was transferred on the London market. This amount has probably increased today by another $20 million. At this rate it will take less than 30 days to find out whether the United States is totally bankrupt. The minister is being unfair to the house and to the country when he gives the impression that we have a new unit of exchange in the International Monetary Fund. The United States dollar is backed by gold and therefore gold is backing the International Monetary Fund. What will happen if United States short term money is recalled and the United States becomes bankrupt? Unless the minister envisages some change in the next few weeks I suggest that with the present trend the United States will be bankrupt within 30 days.
The present rush on gold will surely accelerate. Something will have to be done before the end of next week. Canada must also do something because our exchange is closely tied to the United States dollar. According to some of the remarks made by other hon. members the role played so far by the Bank of Canada has been detrimental.
When we took the limit off interest rates we were told by the minister that interest rates would go down. They have not gone down, they have gone up. They have gone up to the extent that the housing industry is now frozen. In the province of Quebec 600 major producers are leaving because of high interest rates and taking most of their business to the state of Vermont. This surely is a direct result of high interest rates and the instability of our economy.
I agree with the minister when he suggests that Canada is not going to set the gold standard. I am sure he is aware that all the countries involved in the monetary fund rejected the idea suggested at Rio de Janeiro that the United States dollar be used as the basis for international exchange. The only country interested in maintaining the price of gold at $35 per ounce was the United States. I am not

March 14. 1968
Income Tax Act
sure what the result would be if we increased that price to $75, $100 or even higher.
I do know that for years Canada was hoodwinked into believing that it was absolutely necessary to stabilize the price of silver at 97 cents an ounce because that was the desire of the United States. We did not make money as a great silver producer. The United States then passed an act and the price of silver went up to $1.29 per ounce. We continued to produce it for the United States at that price. Some producers got smart, began producing for Britain, and the price of silver rose to $2.46 per ounce. I understand silver is selling on the commercial market for a great deal more. This would indicate that the price of silver is double what the United States is using for the base of its reserve.
The United States is not God Almighty so far as monetary policies are concerned. The United States has been unsuccessful in its negotiations throughout the world in respect of pegging the value of gold. Even with the huge amounts of gold the United States has said it has had over the years, it has been unable to establish stability in respect of its own money. This would indicate the United States has been printing scrip that it never intended to redeem. I think they are doing it with the consent of a number of countries which are now faced with a very serious problem and an almost inevitable calamity.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I ask the minister what he is going to do about this situation. What help can he give the Canadian people if a disaster develops? I calculate that it is not more than two weeks away. I am only guessing but I think that if the International Monetary Fund breaks down and gold is allowed to seek its own level the United States will have a 40-cent dollar. I am also scared that Canada will have a 60-cent dollar, which will mean that Canada will not be able to sell in any market in the world. We will be in a very serious position.
Some of the minister's colleagues may not believe that the situation is serious but I think it is when leaders of the international monetary agencies of the world are spending their Sundays visiting Switzerland not to ski but to sit down and discuss financial matters. These people do not think it is a laughing matter. I am sure those seven or eight people who have been meeting regularly know the limit to which they will be able to back currency in the current situation. I think it is a calamity for us and for the people of the world.

I do not think we will be serving the best interests of the International Monetary Fund or our own best interests if we fail to present what may be an alternative in this situation. I know there are repercussions which I do not understand in the alternative suggested, but I am quite sure everyone will agree that if the price of gold were to double there would be a great deal less interest in moving it around and keeping it under the bed. Speculation is what is moving gold around, not its value.
I believe that people in other countries and United States citizens are involved in this speculation. When people see a very serious economic situation developing which will affect them they hedge, just as the Canadian government has hedged to a limited degree. The minister should not appear to be amused by this situation or try to pass it off. A serious calamity may befall the world in the next few days. If it does occur it will make the Viet Nam war back-page news rather than front-page news. We will not need to withdraw the supply of nickel; that problem will be solved. The Vietnamese will find themselves well off.
The people who are buying gold are not stupid. They also have money, which is very important in the world of economics. These people are going to the London market and buying gold in very large quantities. They are buying $200 million worth of gold a day. This is a very large transaction. In my opinion it is not countries that are buying gold but individuals, corporations and companies interested in hedging in this way.
Perhaps the hon. member for Villeneuve did not give us the answer to the problem but I think what he said is well worth looking at. We will have to make ourselves less dependent on the United States economy or we will find ourselves very hurt by an economic collapse in the international monetary field. We may be hurt even more than the Americans who have perhaps precipitated this kind of collapse.
The Americans appear to have $10 billion worth of gold. If it is sold at the rate of a quarter of a billion dollars a day it will last only 40 days. If the buying of gold accelerates as it has in the past few days, a calamity would easily develop in the next 10 days.

Mr. Chairman, before the minister rises to say something on this rather intriguing question of the price of gold and the mythological claim which gold seems to have on mankind, I should like to ask him to comment on two propositions. First of all, is
March 14, 1968

it not true that if the United States were to raise the price of gold every other nation would also devalue its currency in the same proportion and we would be back in the same boat where we started? Second, what would happen if the United States unilaterally decided to stop buying and selling gold at the price of $35 an ounce and let it find its own level as a monetary metal? It seems to me to be absurd to some extent, when the United States has a gross national product of some $800 billion, that a world monetary crisis of this nature can be brought on by a balance of payments deficit of only $3 billion.
I represent a gold mining constituency and naturally we are very interested in what happens to the price of gold. But it seems to me that a great deal of the discussion this afternoon has been a little far out so far as my understanding of the economics of gold is concerned. It is my understanding that what really makes a nation wealthy and powerful is not the amount of gold it has but the extent of its productive capacity. Gold itself does not produce anything. The people working in the factories and the products they produce are the real key. I ask the minister to comment on those two propositions.

Mr. Chairman, some of the comments made by the hon. member for Villeneuve and the hon. member for Timiskaming, to which I believe there was a reply from the minister, dealt with the fact that the Canadian dollar was not attached to gold in any way, shape or form. I should like to illustrate to hon. members just how true this is. Because of all the hullabaloo about the purchase of gold that is going on in Canada and other places around the world, I thought it would be interesting to find out just how one went about purchasing gold.
I went to the bank and informed them that I was interested in purchasing some gold. In spite of the fact that on the counter there was a big sign which said they bought and sold gold, the first thing the young gentleman who served me said was that they would not take any more orders for gold. I asked him, "What do you mean when you say the bank will not take any more orders for gold?" He said, "We are just not taking any more orders for gold." I asked, "Why?" He said he did not know why. I said, "Can you find out?" He went to find out why they were not taking orders for gold. He brought back another gentleman who then proceeded to try to discourage me from buying gold. He told me that there were
Income Tax Act
storage costs, handling charges and this, that and the other thing.
But I persisted in getting an answer so he went on and even got to the stage of intimating that it was rather unpatriotic to buy gold. I pointed out to him that I happened to be the member of parliament who represents the largest gold producing area on the North American continent and I wondered why it was unpatriotic to buy Canadian gold in a Canadian bank. He changed his tune a little then, and although it took me some two hours and thirty minutes I was able to purchase a little bit of gold.
But the interesting point is that you cannot buy gold for Canadian dollars. You have to go back to your own bank and get the money in American funds. The most interesting point of all is that if you want to store gold in a Canadian bank you also have to pay the storage charges in American dollars. Therefore when the minister says the Canadian dollar is not attached to gold, believe me, Mr. Chairman, he is telling the truth. The trouble is that the Canadian dollar happens to be tied to the American dollar and the American dollar happens to be tied to gold, or it has been until now.
Where does the gold come from?

I made this inquiry of the gentleman at the bank. He said they did not have any here and would have to send to Toronto for it. I said, "Suppose they have not any there; what will you do?" He said they would have to send to the mint for it. Apparently the mint may also be out of gold because it is processed in London, England. A few years ago we had over 200 producing gold mines in this country. Now we are down to about 25 and a number of those are closing this year. But still we have to send to England if we want to buy Canadian gold in Canada and we have to use American money.

Yes.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I do not mind lugging it as long as I know

where to get it. I think that the point raised by the hon. member for Timiskaming is a valid one. I have followed this situation very closely because I have been very interested in gold and I have tried to study the problem and the intricacies of the trading in gold on the international market over the years. The headlines today speak of the buying rush on gold in London, Paris and Zurich which has reached panic proportions. When the same thing happened before Christmas the international financiers were able to cool off the rush a little. Early in January, there was another run and again they were able to cool it off. Last week it started again and over the week end there was a big meeting of the Group of Ten in Switzerland. They came out with a joint statement that they were going to hold the line. However, this time it has had no effect. The panic started on Monday, continued yesterday and increased further today.
Unless I am mistaken and unless all the signs all over the world mean nothing, it would appear to me that by this week end and no later one of two things must be done. Either the price of gold will have to be raised to a meaningful level or gold will have to be demonetized. I am not sure what effect the raising of the price of gold would have. It was done in the 1930's one country at a time. What happened then was that gold moved from one country to another. If it is done sensibly at this time, what will happen will be that the International Monetary Fund will adjust all the currencies to a meaningful value. If they try to demonetize gold, then, unless the minister has more information and a greater understanding of the situation than I have, there will be utter and complete chaos in the world because, as I mentioned before, for 5,000 years people in this world have been looking for a substitute for gold, and as things have progressed over the years some countries within their boundaries have learned to manage without gold.
History has shown to us that paper money is nothing more than paper which can be used to plaster walls. It has to have some other value before it can be accepted and before it has the trust and faith of the nations of the world for use in international commerce which is so necessary in the world today.
I say again, Mr. Chairman, that not later than this week end some decision must be made or the world will face a depression which will make the one in the 1930's look like a garden party.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to put one or two brief and simple questions to the minister. I do not think this is the time for us to go into an extensive examination of the reform of our monetary system which, after all, has served Canada rather well in the last two decades. But I should like to ask the minister whether I am correct in my understanding of what he has said in his responses to questions and indeed in his speeches to the house and to the committee. As I understand it, first, our trade position is excellent and currently it is improving. Second, our dollar is buoyant. Indeed, if it were free it would probably tend upward. Third, fiscally speaking we are now very nearly in balance. According to some independent assessments, we are in balance or even better at present. My question is: Why do we tax now? If I understand the minister correctly, his answer is that we tax: (a) in order that Canada will not have to borrow more in what is obviously a capital-scarce market and thereby further inflate interest rates and complicate other borrowing in Canada and, (b) in order to curb consumer purchases so as to reduce inflation. Am I being too simplistic in the reasons which I advance for the government's action in coming to the country at this time for this not very substantial sum of money? Are these the reasons? Is this the situation?

Mr. Chairman, I just want to ask the minister a couple of questions. I should like to say first, however, that I was interested in noting that he said he had not been converted by the hon. member for Vil-leneuve. If the hon. member for Villeneuve cannot convert him I suggest that he might go back and read the speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs on debt free money made in February, 1963, and consult his colleagues who voted for a resolution on debt free money. This might give him all the explanations he needs in order to support the position of the hon. member for Villeneuve.
My sole purpose in rising is to say that I hope that in the course of this discussion the minister will make some statement which, if possible, will assuage the fears of the Canadian people with respect to the present critical situation in the international money markets. I recognize the minister's difficulties. The minister is dealing with a very delicate mechanism. He wants to say nothing that will make the situation worse, nor is he in a position to make forecasts when all the factors are not known.
March 14, 1968

However, it seems to me that the people of this country have some right to know what the government's plans are and what the government is striving to do. Most of us have the feeling that many of the governments and peoples of the world are like a mesmerized rabbit watching the snake getting closer and closer, and no one seems to know what to do about it. For months now we have watched the gold hoarders, the speculators and the Swiss bankers buying gold and raiding the United States dollar. The situation is approaching the breaking point.
The hon. member for Leeds spoke about our buoyant dollar. If our dollar is buoyant I do not know why the Bank of Canada had to put up some $474 million in the months of January and February in order to keep the Canadian dollar from collapsing. It could not have been very buoyant at that time. Certainly our dollar, and I do not say it with any glee, is under the same pressure as are the United States dollar and the British pound. I am not trying to allocate blame. What I am asking is that we face up to the reality of the situation.
I do not profess to be an authority on international finance, but basing myself on whatever study I have done of the international monetary theory it seems to me that the problem which has been facing the world for several years now and will face us increasingly in the next few months is the problem of the contracting world liquidity. Our international situation is very much like the situation that countries faced domestically in the early 1930's, namely, that in countries which were on the gold standard the medium of exchange was not expanding as rapidly as the economy. There was a period in the 1930's when we had an abundance of goods and people who needed the goods but we lacked a medium of exchange. When we moved from the gold standard to a managed currency within each country such as we have today we managed to provide the medium of exchange by which people could do business. Now, on an international basis, we have not been able to provide this flexible medium of international exchange. As a matter of fact, not only has world liquidity not been keeping pace with the growing trade in the world but it is now likely to contract.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I believe most authorities estimate that the devaluation of the British pound wiped out $1 billion worth of world liquidity. If the United States carries out its intention this year of
Income Tax Act
balancing its payments, this will wipe out some $3 billion worth of world liquidity. Contraction of world liquidity could precipitate very serious problems for international trade. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the world will have to think very seriously about how it can expand world liquidity to keep pace with increasing demand.
However, what I want to ask the minister is this. What prospect is there of getting some agreement reasonably soon among the members of the I.M.F. with respect to supplementary drawing rights? Also, what prospect is there of getting some agreed unit of international monetary exchange? It seems to me that this is the only hope.
I know that this question has been discussed at meetings of ministers of finance of the member nations of the I.M.F., and I understand there was some resistance to it, which I think is unfortunate. I should like to know where the resistance comes from. Is there any hope that in light of the present crisis this resistance will be withdrawn? Is there any prospect that the nations that recognize the need for what I would call a managed international currency would be prepared to proceed without, say, France, which has strenuously opposed this change? Is there any hope that the process that would normally have been left until next October can be speeded up? Frankly, Mr. Chairman, I do not think that we have until next October. If the minister is reasonably optimistic then he will relieve my mind and the minds of a lot of people in Canada, but I doubt that we have until next October.
Are there any emergency measures that can be taken in this regard? Is anything being done to bring the ministers of finance together at an early date in the hope of working out a solution? If the minister can give us any hope or reason for optimism I can assure the minister that he will set a lot of people's minds at ease at a time when there is considerable concern, in some quarters even consternation.

Mr. Chairman I shall be brief as I have ony a few specific questions to direct to the hon. minister.
Here is the first one: Why is manipulating allowed as regards the interest rate of the Bank of Canada? Why was the Bank of Canada able for about twenty years to maintain a stable rate of interest so as to guarantee a

kind of economy which could be termed stable? But since 1945, namely since the manipulating as regards the interest rate of the Bank of Canada, the economy has been completely unbalanced. That is the reason why the interest rate has no limits and is out of control.
I should like the hon. minister to give us explanations as regards the interest rate maintained by the Bank of Canada and the high interest rate due to manipulating. In a word, why, once again, this manipulating of the interest rate?
That is the question I am directing to the hon. minister. If he will be so kind as to answer, I will have further questions to ask him afterwards.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on this question. I think that gold backing for the United States dollar is a myth. All currencies of the world are based on the United States dollar. If the price of gold was changed all currencies would also change in proportion.
A few weeks ago the amount of money circulating in the United States was $181 billion. The United States currency is not only a domestic currency but an international currency. United States currency can be spent in Europe. In the United States a dollar is a dollar. In Canada a dollar is a dollar. However, in Europe a United States dollar is no longer a dollar but a gold dollar.
To my mind, trying to prevent people from buying gold is a little out of line. The United States is contending that the price of gold should not be raised. We must remember that $750 million worth of gold each year does not enter the monetary system at all; it is going into industry and into the arts. Although General de Gaulle was blamed last year for taking gold out of the United States, I understand he did not take one cent's worth out of that country. The United States is losing gold to people all over the world. These people want to protect their investments. They are called sharpers, dishonest and unpatriotic. But money itself, Mr. Chairman, is not patriotic.
Gold does not come from the United States alone. The United States is mining only about one-third of the gold that is used in industry and the arts in that country. The United States is also using a lot of gold in its space program. The electronics industry also uses gold. This gold is procured from countries other than the United States. They are even getting it from Canada. We shut down our
[Mr. Latullppe.l
gold mines because we do not charge a proper price for the gold.
Where can you find any industry today, Mr. Chairman, that buys its raw materials at 1934 prices? I well remember the depression of 1929 which to my mind was brought about by the United States policy toward gold. The United States had gathered in gold from all round the world. This led to speculation in the United States. I remember that at that time currencies all over the world were dislocated.
I think my hon. friend across the aisle is wrong in what he says, because it was only after President Roosevelt established the price of gold at $35 an ounce that the currencies of the world were adjusted and countries were able to conduct business. I was in business at that time and if that price had not been established when it was, in six months we would have gone into bankruptcy because three-quarters of our products were exported. I remember that what happened was a direct result of the gold situation.
I cannot understand why our friends across the way want to substitute something else for gold. What they want is "paper gold". How is the United States going to finance the Viet Nam war unless it is with this paper gold? They cannot use real gold because they have not sufficient reserves. So they issue paper and call it paper gold, but you cannot get gold for it. It is not right to call that paper gold, but that is what they do.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I cannot understand that attitude. For my part I say, let us stick to gold at least while the Viet Nam war is on. I think this question definitely should be looked into. When we are paying $15 million a year in subsidies to our gold mines I do not see why we should sell the product of our gold mines to the United States for $35 an ounce, a price that was established in 1934.
When President Roosevelt established that price in 1934 people everywhere told him that this action would raise prices in the United States. It did no such thing. Prices before and after the gold hike were practically the same with the exception of some imports. But what did that action do? It restored world trade and world trade restored prices. That is exactly what we are up against today. The question is one of liquidity.
We need liquidity and we are not getting it. No matter what you say about gold, it is the base for credit. Some say that the International Monetary Fund has old-fashioned ideas. When Canada puts up $100 million, the fund

asks for $25 million of that subscription to be in gold. Why is that done? Paper credits are expanding but the relative gold base for our money is going the other way. The United States is saying to European countries, "You have $15 billion in gold in your reserves." At the same time any United States economist will tell you that the purchasing power of the United States dollar will decrease from 4 to 5 per cent in 1968. I presume the Canadian dollar will follow that decline. Personally I do not think we can do anything about that inflation. Despite the so-called new economics we have in today's world, I do not think we can do anything about it because for a long time we have had inflation and we are going to have inflation. It has now become a question of the degree of inflation we are to have. But the United States is telling Europe, "You have got $15 billion in gold locked up in the common market and in 1968 the purchasing power of your gold is going down from 4 to 5 per cent." I ask you, who is going to believe that?
Some say that all we need to do nowadays is issue paper currency. If gold values are to be kept to the level of paper currency values, by and by your paper currency will be worthless and your gold will be worthless. That is ridiculous. People do not believe that gold is worthless. People think and have always thought that gold is the store of value.
The other day a young woman in Toronto took her savings out of her bank to buy gold. She thought she was protecting her investment; she was getting out of paper and into gold. People all over the world are thinking the same way. When a woman in India buys a gold bracelet it is because she does not trust the bank with her money and trusts gold. From the year 1340 gold has been on the upward trend. And in a while its price has reached a plateau but its price has always crept up. It has never gone down.
All the United States has to do if it wants to get out of the jam it is in is to say, "We will not buy or sell gold at $35 an ounce." That is all there is to it and it could do it within the framework of the International Monetary Fund. The president need not go to congress. In fact, I do not see why he should. I do not see why we have to defend the Canadian dollar. It is pegged at 92| cents United States. Incidentally, much of my information comes from New York international reports. When the Canadian dollar moves down three-quarters of a cent it has got to be defended by the Bank of Canada,
Income Tax Act
but if we had a flexible exchange rate there would be no need to defend it. In the 1920's our dollar went down at one time to 76 cents United States and within one year of that it was selling at a premium. Why did things happen that way? When your dollar goes down the tariff barriers against you go down at the same time. Your exports increase and your imports decrease. It is as simple as that. The marketplace supplies the answer.
I would say that the United States is defending its dollar to save face only. It is saying that an increase in the price of gold would benefit mainly Russia and South Africa. Russia has no store of gold and neither has South Africa. The South African mines produce about $1 billion worth of gold each year but the South Africans use that money to buy commodities all round the world. That action increases international trade. As for Russia, at present they are using their funds for spaceships, armies and navies. If they had twice the amount of gold they would be over here buying pins and needles and the sort of stuff the people in Russia want.
Leaving out Russia and South Africa for the moment, it is obvious that if the price of gold were increased the approximately $42 billion of gold in the western world would double or triple in value. I was reading a book written about 120 years ago by a French economist. He said that the only way to find the price of gold is to see how much gold will buy how much silver. France at that time was on the silver standard. Applying that measurement to gold prices, gold today should be worth $105 an ounce because the price of silver has also gone up.
As for this talk of gold being a monetary measure, how can gold possibly be a monetary measure when in 1967 no gold went into the central banks? Instead, approximately $750 million worth went into industry. Accordingly, gold is a commodity. Why should it not be traded at commodity prices instead of the price that was fixed in 1934?
I cannot understand the thinking of some people in the opposition. Some of them want this paper gold. I think we have got too much paper. The world is swamped in paper. I think we want some restriction and gold has always applied a restriction. Away back in 1840 the Bank of England was checked for issuing too much paper. They had to get back to gold.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall be brief in replying to the comments which have been made and which have carried us far beyond clause 1 of the bill. I can understand the interest and concern of hon. members in the present international crisis. I first wish to say to hon. members who have spoken that I listened most carefully to their comments. I have been much engaged in thinking about the crisis that has existed for some time and I have devoted a good deal of my attention to considering what would be appropriate action not only for this country but for the collectivity of nations.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
It is a very serious problem. I have been pointing this out to the house over a period of several weeks and it is one reason why I felt it was very desirable we should proceed with the bill before us. It is also the reason for my announcing a number of other measures to be as certain as we can be that we in Canada are not a cause of disturbance and that our defences are well buttressed so that we do not get brought into the centre of this worldwide disturbance. I say this in response to remarks made by my hon. friend from Leeds who made some comments about the position of the Canadian dollar.
As I said earlier in the house, our trade position is very good, our exports are high, our imports are not rising too rapidly. We are now getting our fiscal situation into what I consider to be a sound position and it is generally recognized, as we saw the other day in a statement by the O.E.C.D., that our fiscal policies, particularly the rapidity with which we have been able to adjust them to meet a changing situation, are commended by the international community.

There is no group of nations in the world more important than those that belong to the O.E.C.D. They include all the major industrialized countries, and if they comment that the Canadian economy is strong, that the Canadian dollar is properly priced and that our policies are appropriate to the circumstances, it is a mark in our favour which is not disregarded in the markets of the world. The policies which the O.E.C.D. commended include measures of the kind which are now before us. It has been necessary for us to make it plain to the world that we are determined to maintain a sound economy, this enabling the world as a whole to look at Canada and say: There is a country whose currency is appropriate to its circumstances. I have no hesitation in commending parliament for having taken very seriously the proposals which have been put before it and for discussing today the serious international disturbances which have been engaging our attention.
A number of questions have been asked. I do not think I can answer them all to the satisfaction of the committee but I should like to say something first of all about the relationship between the Canadian dollar, the American dollar and gold. The legal position is that the Canadian dollar is established on the basis of a relationship to the United States dollar and until this relationship is changed whatever happens to the American dollar is reflected in the value of the Canadian dollar. So the sort of comment made by the hon. member for Timiskaming that we might see a 40-cent American dollar and a 60-cent Canadian dollar is not likely to be apposite. The latter at the present time is worth 924 cents United States and until this relationship is changed by Canada, presumably in consultation with and with the approval of the International Monetary Fund, the present relationship will continue.

That relationship is artificial. We have agreed to maintain our dollar at 924 cents. But if something exceptional were to happen to the United States dollar is it not true that the International Monetary Fund could no longer support the present value of the Canadian dollar in terms of the United States dollar? I mentioned a hypothetical situation in which the United States dollar fell seriously in value. The International Monetary Fund could not maintain the present relationship in such circumstances because it would mean the virtual collapse of the fund.
March 14, 1968

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member is talking now about a hypothetical situation which is most unlikely to arise. The United States dollar is the principal reserve currency in the world; it is held by central banks or treasuries, in addition to gold. So one cannot devalue the United States dollar. All one can do is change the price of gold. There is no reason to think that if the price of gold were changed or if any change were made in the relationship between gold and the United States dollar this would necessarily disturb the relationship between other world currencies and the American dollar. This is the view I hold, though I cannot say for certain. The relationship is established by other factors-relative costs, purchasing power, and so on.
In the event the price of gold was raised substantially would this not have a serious effect on world liquidity?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman. This is one of the principal reasons why an increase in the price of gold is not a panacea, not necessarily the best way of dealing with the problem of expanding international liquidity. It seems to me and to other ministers of finance who have studied this question that it would be better to have a controlled increase in international liquidity rather than an arbitrary and indiscriminate increase which would come about as a result of an increase in the price of gold. The benefits of such an increase would depend on how much gold a country held, and we must remember that gold is not distributed equally round the world in proportion to the needs of various countries or even in proportion to their reserves. Some countries, such as France and Switzerland, hold a high proportion of their reserves in gold. Others, such as Canada, hold about half. The proportion varies greatly, so an increase in the price of gold would not provide additional liquidity on the basis of need.
How long can the United States continue to buy gold at $35 an ounce when it costs a great deal more than that to produce it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not like to speculate about the actions of the United States because I am not privy to their councils. As I understand it, United States policy so far has been to maintain the price of gold at $35 an ounce. I should explain that the United States is maintaining this price not only in connection with transactions between central banks which present claims on the federal reserve system
Income Tax Act
when they cash United States dollars but it has also been providing gold at the same price in the London gold market, with the result that there is one price for gold throughout the world. As many hon. members have pointed out, very large amounts of gold have been sold in the London gold market, and this is a reflection of the very serious disturbances going on in which very large amounts of gold are disappearing out of stocks into private hoards.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I shall now deal with the final question, that raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam about the prospects of getting some agreement and why we have had difficulty. The so-called Group of Ten which comprises the ministers of finance of the ten most important financial countries in the world, as one might say, and Canada happens to be included in that Group of Ten, have been working for some time on the creation of a new type of reserve unit. In Rio this year we approved in principle a system of special drawing rights as a supplement to existing reserves of gold and reserve currencies. It had been understood that these new reserve units, whatever they were to be, were not to be used until they were needed. One of the tests is that they would not relieve the United States of the necessity of dealing with its own balance of payments problem. This has been one of the difficult issues. There is no doubt about it that the United States has been in balance of payments difficulties for a period of years, and these have been greatly exacerbated recently by the Viet Nam war and the unwillingness of the United States to impose taxes in order to pay the cost of that war.
I hesitate to say this because I do not mean it as any reflection on the United States-they make their own decisions-but I do think we in this country have been very wise, albeit with some difficulty, in imposing the necessary taxes upon ourselves so that our finances are in good order. There is no doubt about it that one of the reasons the United States is losing gold and one of the reasons it is in balance of payments difficulties is that it has been unwilling to do what we are doing in this parliament, impose taxes so that their fiscal position would be improved. I think that is all I have to say, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be very brief. I would simply like to point out a

March 14. 1968
Income Tax Act
few things which I think might be useful to my colleagues at this stage of the debate.
I listened patiently to all that has been said on this bill and previous measures, and I think we are facing a situation which should be clear to everyone. We are most of us speaking about a problem which we do not understand and about which we have insufficient experience. I feel it is no presumption to say that, in this house, there are perhaps not more than three or four members who have enough experience of the complexities of international finance and I think that they, who know most about that, are the ones who are asking themselves the most questions.
I say, therefore, that this is not the time to pose as experts and try to settle international or national crises, or to promote our respective ideologies, but I believe that the time has come for us to form a kind of sacred union in order to get through the present crisis. I know that, under normal conditions, it is in order for everybody to make suggestions, in our parliamentary system. But, Mr. Chairman, I think we must draw a line, especially when, in a way, our house is burning. When the house is burning, everybody lends a helping hand to put the fire out; one does not sit idly by discussing the best way of putting it out, one acts. One puts the fire out first, and then one discusses the advisability of improving one's methods.
It is in that spirit, Mr. Chairman, that last evening, although I was quite inclined to do like others and play the giddy-goat before the government and to have the satisfaction of voting against a 3 per cent surtax on personal income tax, I told myself that, in such circumstances, one had to think of the superior interests of the country instead of merely considering our electoral interests. I also thought that if we would not co-operate with the government to prevent a worsening of the crisis, those who would particularly suffer the most would again be the small wage-earners, the pensioners who would see the value of the dollar considerably decrease, the unemployed whose number would appreciably increase, the small and average businesses which would be unable to survive. I think that such considerations should have priority over the interest which could lead us to defeat the government, to launch elections and to be in a position to say: Well, it was defeated by us. But at what cost? By a worsening of a situation which could be disastrous for the country.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened to all the representations made in this house by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp); I have reread the appeal made to us by the right hon. Prime Minister. I have read the comments in the press on the pathetic appeal made for the twentieth time by President Johnson of the United States, a country with which we have such close economic ties.
I have also read, in yesterday's edition of La Presse, an article in which the author of the Kiplinger Washington Letter made somber predictions concerning the future of the Canadian dollar. I have listened to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and I should like, in passing, to congratulate him on his moderation and abnegation during a debate in the course of which he could easily have demolished the government by all sorts of demagogic arguments.
In view of all this, I have said to myself: this is not the time to hold interminable discussions. This is a time for nation-wide cooperation, for what we are trying to settle is the future of the country and of our electorate. It is not a matter of knowing whether we are smarter than those in power.
In my opinion, those responsible for the future of my country are members of the government legally in power at present, and I feel that regardless of our political affiliation, we should heed the voice of our conscience and tell ourselves: It is a time for co-operation, it is a time for a sacred union in order to spare Canada a disaster. I urge all my colleagues to put an end to all unprofitable discussions on financial theories and on ways to settle national and international crises. Let us leave it to the government to assume its responsibilities. If it is wrong, we can always call it to account at the next election, but the Canadian people will not be able to blame us for having systematically caused trouble, for selfish reasons, at this critical time.

I have never been persuaded that this was particularly equitable and I was confirmed in this view by the views of the Carter commission, with which my hon. friend's party is apparently in very close agreement.
The members of that commission, after investigating these very proposals, came out very strongly against them on the ground that it was not equitable as between home owners and tenants, and so on. Indeed, the Carter commission almost recommended that the imputed rent on owner-occupied houses should be subject to tax. They wanted to move the other way altogether and tax home owners even more than they are now taxed. This is the view the Carter commission came to. I mention this as further evidence that it is a very arguable proposition whether it is equitable to deduct either property taxes or mortgage interest.
In my case, one of the reasons I live in a house that I own rather than an apartment is

You are lucky not to have a mortgage. How did you reach that stage? It is interesting that the minister has finally found something in the Carter commission report to which he can attach himself. It is obviously a peculiarly isolated attachment to one aspect only of the Carter commission report. As I understand it, the proposals of the Carter commission related to a total picture and a total package. The commission did not consider land taxes in isolation and look at them all by themselves. What is required is that we look at the total tax structure as it has grown up in Canada. This is what the Carter commission did and it came to a number of conclusions with regard to that total picture.
The commissioner was considering the total picture of the tax structure in Canada when he talked about the favouritism that exists in the tax structure with respect to a number of industries in this country. The commissioner also came to the conclusion that we should consider a dollar of income as a dollar liable to taxation. It was in this context that the Carter commission made its report. Therefore the fact that the minister extracts from the report of that commission a particular view with which he happens to agree does not in the total sense, I think, make that view invalid and it does not give him grounds for advancing it as a reason for disregarding or discarding the concept about which we are talking.
If I own a home and rent a room or own an apartment block and rent apartments I can deduct for taxation purposes the expenditures incurred by me in running whatever business I am running, whether it is renting one room or renting a whole apartment block. Included in these expenses are land taxes. It is quite true that in this sense the corporation that owns a block of apartments or the individual renting a suite extracts from the tenants sufficient money to help pay the total bill and leave a profit. But the tenants do not receive any consideration in their rent because the individual who owns the building is able to deduct the amount he pays in property taxes and on maintenance and the like. The owner of the house or apartment block can deduct these things from his tax bill.

I intend to oppose this clause in the same way as we have opposed every suggestion by this government and this minister to raise taxes at this time. Obviously, for 1968 the minister is proposing solutions for Canada's economic troubles that have been proposed by practically every government since the 1920's, when the economy has been in trouble. Those solutions failed then and, inevitably, this solution will fail now.
The minister says that the way to cure our ills is to increase taxes and decrease the purchasing power of the Canadian people. Inevitably that must lead to greater unemployment. Deliberately the minister is following policies that will foster greater unemployment.
Recent figures released by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics relating to the Department of Manpower and Immigration prove that what we said a few months ago, when the minister first made his proposals, has come true. For the benefit of committee members I shall read these figures, contained in an article which appeared in todays Ottawa Journal:
Unemployment in February rose to 482,000, up 18,000 from January, and represented 6.4 per cent of the labor force, highest level since March of 1964 .. .
The February unemployment figure was 86,000 higher than the same month of last year ...
The February percentage of unemployed, 6.4, compared with 6.1 per cent in January and 5.4 per cent in February of last year. Two years ago the February rate was five per cent.
The increased personal and corporation taxes undoubtedly will increase the numbers of unemployed. An examination of the regional figures shows what difficulties we are heading into. In the Atlantic provinces 67,000 in

February were unemployed. In Quebec, 179,000 were unemployed early this year; in Ontario there were 130,000, on the prairies 48,000 and in British Columbia 58,000.

Unemployment is rising everywhere and the policies the minister is following will make the situation even worse.
Opposition to what the minister is doing has come from many sources. Last month the Canadian Labour Congress and the Confederation of National Trade Unions made their annual submissions to the government. While these two organizations have differences about such matters as Bill C-186, their submissions with regard to economic and social matters are remarkable in their similarity. After all, the brother of the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development was the secretary of the Confederation of National Trade Unions, and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration was president of that confederation before he came here as a cabinet minister. I see the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development in his place. I wish to put on record what that confederation has said, because it bears directly on the proposals we are discussing today. The Confederation of National Trade Unions advocated yesterday stimulation rather than restraint of the economy, which it described as socially anarchic. The C.N.T.U. urged the recreation of a prices board and institution of some of the main proposals of the Carter royal commission on taxation.
