The briefs submitted by the Confederation of National Trade Unions and by the Canadian Labour Congress, both endorsing the basic proposals of the Carter commission and urging the government to implement them now, show clearly the line taken by these organizations which between them represent almost two million Canadians who work for wages.
Instead of doing this, the minister tells us that because we are in financial difficulties a surcharge of 3 per cent on personal income tax must be levied, accompanied by an increase in corporation taxes. Rather than implement the Carter commission report the hon. gentleman is penalizing those who are already paying more than they ought to pay. At the same time he allows those corporations which are in the select group of resource based industries to get away scot free, as they have all the time.
In addition, the minister and the Prime Minister have sought to create the impression that the reason for our difficulties at the present time is that we have permitted wage increases which are unreasonably large, in excess of the ability of the economy to stand, more than the increase in our productivity justifies, and so on. The Prime Minister said in his speech-and I quote from page 7 of the press release giving the text:
Corporation profits, which in the early years of expansion had risen strongly to relatively high levels, have, however, declined significantly in the course of the past two years.
That is true. But I wish that in the years when corporation profits were high, back in

1965 and 1966, we had heard from the Prime Minister, as well as from the president of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Rasminsky, who has also been making appeals for restraint lately, appeals directed to the corporations along the lines of those we hear today directed to workers and trade unionists urging them to exercise restraint and common sense.
One example of the inability or refusal of the government to urge restraint on those who ought to show it is the case which came up a couple of months ago when first Noran-da Copper, then International Nickel and Hudson Bay Mining increased the price of copper by more than 25 per cent. Members of this party raised the matter with the Minister of Finance who promised to look into the situation.
He did so, and eventually we got a statement from the Minister of Trade and Commerce in which the hon. gentleman explained that world prices of copper had risen to such an extent that a 25 per cent increase in prices in Canada by the companies I have mentioned was actually quite moderate. The fact is that the profits of those private companies have never been as high as they are at the present time. But they did not feel called upon to exercise any restraint. After all, there is a war on in Viet Nam, there is a fantastic demand for copper, there is a copper strike in progress in the United States, removing domestic producers in that country from the picture, so why not get all the market will bear? Accordingly they raised their prices by more than 25 per cent. And what did the Minister of Trade and Commerce say, speaking for the government? The increase, he told us, was quite a reasonable one and the companies were acting reasonably.
In the face of this attitute I suggest that the proposal of the government for the establishment of a board to look into prices and, I suppose, into wages-certainly not into profits, because it would be too much to expect this government to appoint a board to look into exorbitant profits made by corporations-will prove as useless and as fruitless an effort as most of the measures the minister has put forward.

These special interests have done a wonderful job in confusing the Canadian public. According to them one would think the Carter commission was a group of wild eyed socialists who had no experience with business, who know nothing about the tax system or about anything else. The facts are the exact opposite. The Carter commission was appointed in 1962 by the Conservative government under the leadership of the right hon. member for Prince Albert. Mr. Kenneth Carter was a former director of the Canadian Tax Foundation. The commission hired a large staff of competent, well trained experts who spent about three years making their studies. The study cost $3J million, and the report has been greeted with approval by everybody except the Minister of Finance and the special interests who, it seems to me, he is here to represent and to defend.
The Carter commission on taxation found that essentially Canada has an unfair tax system. It found that billions of dollars of income are escaping tax altogether, or enjoying tax privileges which make the burden of taxation on the rest of the people of Canada that much greater. It recommended lower taxes for income groups making less than $10,000 a year, and higher taxes for those making over $10,000 a year, and taxes for persons making capital gains. The commission's recommendations would have benefited 95 per cent of the people of Canada. Conversely they would have hurt the 5 per cent who get special privileges under the present tax system. Naturally we heard ad nauseam from the 5 per cent as to the inequities and iniquities in the proposals of the Carter commission.
While these special interests represent only 5 per cent of the people of Canada obviously they have the ear of the Minister of Finance and of the government because the minister has found innumerable reasons to ignore the

What did the Carter commission find out? As I said a moment ago, it found out that the present taxation system does not afford fair taxation for all Canadians. It found that the present tax structure has led to Canadians being less well off, through the lack of goods and services that could be provided by more efficient use of labour, capital and natural resources. Is it that our governments are so driven by the gold craze that they forget what is going on here, what happens to our population? The Quebec premier Mr. Johnson, said that there was only one solution and I use his own expression: Let Ottawa hand over some taxes to the provinces. But Ottawa will not let go: it is trapped in a struggle to save the dollar. Not to save the individuals or the unemployed, no: to save the dollar.

In the United States it is gold, here it is the dollar. We must save the dollar. No matter if citizens are stripped of everything, if what they have left is taken away from them, if there is unemployment and misery. We must save the dollar. Let us save the dollar.
Things have reached a point where this government's slogan is: The dollar must be saved, gold must be saved. As for the citizen, no matter. There are 179,000 unemployed in Quebec, that is 8.4 per cent of the total, and that is of no importance. There is no time to think of that: the dollar must be saved, gold must be saved.
Mr. Chairman, it makes one wonder whether the government is not a little panic-stricken in the present situation. Why does the government not wage the same fight to save the individual, the Canadian citizen, as it wages to save the dollar? It is very important in a period of crisis to save the individual also. When I see this fight to save the dollar, I wonder what is wrong with Canada that we are forced to wage such a big fight? What could be the reason for such a crisis? Why an economic crisis?
Have potatoes stopped growing in Canada, as the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) would say? Have cows stopped giving milk, and caused an economic crisis? Have hens stopped giving eggs? Has production decreased in our pulp mills, our industries? Has production stopped? No, Mr. Chairman, we are able to produce as much as before. Our industry, our agriculture can be as flourishing as they were. There is no crisis in those areas.
Our workers are not refusing to work. They are willing to carry on; they are ready to make every effort. Our dealers are willing to keep on selling: they have goods to sell. They are not short of goods. In proof of that, there are sales everywhere. Our natural resources are still there. We are still able to tap and develop them. Why, then, a crisis of the dollar?
The average citizen, Mr. Chairman, has a right to wonder why there is a dollar crisis, when our natural resources are still there, our industries are still there, our citizens are still doing their duty to produce, our businessmen are still ready to sell and Canadian citizens are ready to buy as much and even more than yesterday.

to devaluating the real resource, production, to be in a better position to control it.
When a country gets prosperous, there are financiers who endeavour to control its industries, its businesses, its economy. They try to reduce the prices of those industries, to be in a better position to buy them, to control them, as was done during the 1929 depression.
Economy was thriving then. The dollar collapsed overnight, and great international trusts, big international corporations took control of our Canadian industries and succeeded in developing them to their own advantage.
From 1929 to 1939, at a time of another dollar crisis, and not an industrial crisis, some international trusts succeeded in getting the control of our large electric power companies, our pulp and paper mills, our major industries and, at the present time, they want to start the same game all over again.
Mr. Chairman, we are told there is a crisis, but I do not believe there is a real crisis. It is only in the minds of those who administer our economic and monetary system. The dollar crisis exists only in the minds of those who manage our monetary system, that is, in the mind of our Minister of Finance, the governor of the Bank of Canada and a few others, because there is no real crisis. We still have our natural resources, our resources, our workers in a position to produce and our citizens who can buy. It seems to me quite clear, Mr. Chairman.
Now, why is there a crisis at the present time? What have we done to be the victims of a crisis which we did not want? What is at fault in Canada that we are suddenly engulfed in a crisis? What happened?
Gold, Mr. Chairman. But for the past 28 years, our money has not been based on gold. It was a minister of finance of the Liberal government in 1940, Mr. Ilsley, who stated in 1940 that the value of the Canadian dollar was no longer based on gold.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
Our dollar is not based on gold. Then why? Would it be on account of the monetary crisis in the United States, in Europe, in Great Britain or elsewhere? Now, since our dollar is no longer based on gold, why should we suddenly experience a crisis? Why should we be the victims of a crisis with which we have nothing to do?
It would be about time for our Minister of Finance to solve the problems of which he is responsible and he should refrain, moreover,
Income Tax Act
from trying to solve the problems of others and plunging us in a crisis which does not concern us.
He says that the solution is higher taxes. That is not a solution, Mr. Chairman. On the contrary, it will only create a problem, because if the federal government, the provinces, the municipalities and the school boards raise their taxes, we will be showered by taxes, as they say, and the people, who bear the brunt of it, will be the victims of a crisis brought about by our Minister of Finance, who wants everybody to impose taxes. Other countries may be faced with a crisis, but it should not affect us because our dollar is no longer based on gold. However, there will soon be a crisis in Canada if everybody starts imposing more and more taxes.
Therefore, I am opposed to clause 4 of this bill, because there is no reason for this tax. Furthermore, this tax will help to bring about a real crisis which will affect the whole Canadian people. Mr. Johnson said yesterday: There is only one solution: let Ottawa lower its taxes. However, there is another solution: if Ottawa does not want to lower its taxes, let Quebec lower its own.

speechtext: In order to ensure the orderly discussion of the estimates, we are now considering the vote of the Board of Broadcast Governors. This will be handled by the Secretary of State. If it is agreeable, following the carrying of that item, if this is done tonight, I should like to call all of the items under the name of the Secretary of State. I hope that will be agreeable.
Agreed.
She is not running.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee was last considering this item a few days ago I was making some remarks about the extent of the improvements that I had detected in public affairs programming on C.B.C. television in recent months. I gave credit where I believed it was justified and made the point that I felt the Beryl Fox documentary on Viet Nam last Sunday night on C.B.C. television entitled "Last Reflections on a War" was a poignantly moving and beautiful experience. In my opinion it was a much better balanced program on Viet Nam than any I had seen previously on C.B.C. television, much better balanced than the previous C.B.C. television studies of Viet Nam.
I then moved on to what will be the concluding phase of my remarks, to say a word or two about the Board of Broadcast Governors and the passing of an era in Canadian broadcasting. The era of the B.B.G. is being

phased out fairly soon and we will move into the era of the Canadian Radio-Television Commission, which will be the main supervisory authority in this field. I felt that a hail and farewell to the B.B.G., and particularly to its distinguished president and chairman, Dr. Andrew Stewart, was in order at this time.
Dr. Stewart came to broadcasting a virtual, or at least a comparative stranger. He came from the field of education to an industry of which he obviously possessed great knowledge and for which he obviously possessed great sensitivity. None the less it was an industry with which he had no direct connection. He brought to it, I suggest, Mr. Chairman, a rare dedication, a fine wit and a keen academic mind. He presided over the licensing and the control and authority-dispensing functions of broadcasting in Canada in one of its most exciting and explosive periods, when the so-called second stations entered Canada's major television markets. I refer to the new private stations that now constitute in large part the Canadian television network. Dr. Stewart, as head of the B.B.G., witnessed the inception of this new era in Canadian broadcasting, the era of private television operations and of competition in the major Canadian broadcasting markets.
I submit that as head of the B.B.G. he served both as father and as nurse to what are still comparatively new offspring. They are now testing and venturing upon new ground, but I am sure they are destined to fulfil a great role and serve a great purpose in Canadian national and cultural life in the years ahead.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I think the stations that came into being then, and all those connected with them, owe Dr. Stewart a debt of gratitude for the sagacity and sensitivity he displayed during the first difficult years of competitive television in this country. At all times in my experience Dr. Stewart ruled with understanding and responsibility. I join with my colleagues in this house in saluting Dr. Stewart for the contribution he made to broadcasting in Canada, as his board, the Board of Broadcast Governors, is phased out to be replaced by the new broadcasting authority. I suggest that the new chief of the Canadian Radio-Television Commission could do worse than mark the footsteps of the good doctor and tread in them boldly.
In the field of broadcasting in this country we stand on the threshold of an exciting era, of unexplored frontiers, when all Canadians,
Maich 14, 1968

because of the nature of the industry and of this country, will be integrally involved in Canadian broadcasting and affected every day of their lives by what is done by broadcasters. One case in point is educational television, or instructional television, a subject with which the standing committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts has been studiously engaged for the past several weeks, and in connection with which that committee has been examining a wide variety of witnesses who have come to Ottawa to present to committee members their knowledge and expertise in this field.
The frontiers of Canadian E.T.V. have hardly been approached, let alone crossed. There are great chapters ahead for educational television in Canada. This is one area in which the new officers of the C.R.T.C., this new broadcasting authority, will be vitally interested. So, speaking for myself, I hope it will be possible for the views of Dr. Andrew Stewart and other members of the Board of Broadcast Governors to be made available to the standing committee on broadcasting while it is continuing its study of E.T.V. and before any long range policy in the field of educational television is formulated. All of us on the standing committee look forward to the soon to be announced appointments to the Canadian Radio-Television Commission. And we look forward to working with the new executive officers of the new broadcasting body in order to buttress and improve broadcasting in this country.
I conclude by reiterating my thankfulness and appreciation for the work that Dr. Stewart and the B.B.G. have done, a feeling that I am sure is shared by everyone in this chamber, and by expressing the firm belief that the new C.R.T.C. authority will continue in its predecessor's most instructive footsteps.

Mr. Chairman, the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg South, in contrast with those of other members of his party in the house in weeks gone by, are refreshing. The Conservative party has usually used any occasion on which we discuss broadcasting to castigate the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I am sure that we all at some time or other, when viewing C.B.C. programs, have heard views expressed with which we do not agree. That is understandable, because by its nature the C.B.C. must try to please everyone in Canada, and obviously that cannot be done all the time. Consequently from time to time all of us shall see programs which we find objectionable.
Supply-C.B.C.
Regretfully, I say, we have not seen any element of reasonableness or balance in the Conservative party's approach to public broadcasting in this nation. Their criticisms have all been onesided and that is why the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg South sounded so refreshing. But no matter how often he expresses his views, new, fundamental views, perhaps, they will not undo the damage that has resulted from an unreasoned and unreasonable condemnation of the public broadcasting system by his party's members.
When the legislation establishing the Board of Broadcast Governors was introduced, and the old board of C.B.C. governors was to be replaced, a Conservative government was in office. That legislation was alluded to by practically everyone who supported it as the salvation of broadcasting in Canada. Credit should be given where credit is due. The man who piloted that legislation through the house was a highly respected, honoured and loved member. Practically everyone, regardless of party, held him in high esteem. I am referring to the late George Nowlan.
Regardless of the qualities of the then new legislation to establish the Board of Broadcast Governors, all was not well. All on the government side alluded to the bill as bringing in a most necessary organizational structure which would save Canadians from the denigrating effects that television and radio would have if they were allowed to go on unfettered and uncontrolled.
It is interesting to see how appointments to that new Board of Broadcast Governors, which was established by the Conservative government, were made. The board was loaded with people whose only qualification for sitting on it was that they were Conservatives or Conservative supporters. Perhaps that is why the Conservative party now find it necessary to condemn public broadcasting in Canada. The board which the Conservative party established was abortive. Those who sat on it knew nothing about broadcasting. The Conservatives loaded the board with people who had no real conscience or determination with respect to making public broadcasting a worth-while venture in Canada. The Conservatives loaded that board with political appointees. In fact, at one stage during those years, while for some purpose a national conference of Conservatives was being held in the Chateau Laurier here in Ottawa, there were in attendance goodly numbers of young delegates and young gentlemen whose purpose appeared to be, not the business of the

March 14, 1968
Supply-C.B.C.
conference itself but to search out individuals within the Conservative ranks in government who could provide a television licence. Again we saw the emergence of the lowest form of political involvement in the field of public broadcasting.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Like your relationship with the C.L.C.

If the hon. member who made that comment would like to ask me a question, so that I could hear it, I would gladly yield him the floor for that purpose. Or if he would like to take the floor himself I would be glad to listen to him. I do not see any takers. The hon. member who just interrupted must be one of those whom the Minister of Agriculture labelled yesterday as one whose watermelon was more important than his head.
Filibuster.

I know, Mr. Chairman, that you are concerned about the enforcement of the rules. I do not call upon you to protect me from these members who are yaking away for some unknown purpose. I am simply saying that if there is difficulty in Canada with respect to broadcasting, the Conservative party must bear the brunt of the blame because it was the Conservative party which sought to establish a Board of Broadcast Governors for the sole purpose of providing havens for its own political supporters. As a consequence, regardless of the merits which might have been inherent in the structure set-up, it could not operate with any effectiveness because it was loaded with political hacks. These are the facts. No wonder hon. gentlemen to my right take objection to the truth when it comes home to them.
I want to say with respect to public broadcasting that I am not one of those who are addicted to television viewing. Indeed if there were a scale I would be on the other end of it, inasmuch as I do not particularly like television as a medium of communication or entertainment; I seldom take the opportunity of viewing it. But I do enjoy radio and especially I enjoy the C.B.C.'s radio broadcasting.
Over the years I have enjoyed listening to those programs which have always been of extremely high quality, and show evidence of fine programming, ranging all the way from the early morning news and views, including Max Ferguson's contribution, which I am sure, is a delight to all of us, to the more

serious evening programs. Naturally there are programs which do not please everybody; any organization such as the C.B.C. which tries to deal with the Canadian population in total cannot please all the people all the time. But on balance the radio programs emanating from the C.B.C. are as fine this year as they were in years past and deserve a large measure of commendation and support.
I hear an hon. member use the word "filibuster"; I hear this word in the background. If any in this parliament over the last five years-I am not talking about right now-are liable to a charge of filibustering, it is the people in the Conservative ranks.
Know all.

They do not like the truth; it is too bad. They do not enjoy listening to it. We only need look at the progress made in considering broadcasting legislation itself. I understand there was agreement that if the broadcasting bill introduced this session was referred to a committee for close and essential examination, as it was, it would be considered in the house with a minimal amount of discussion. This was one of those gentlemen's agreements which are made. Yet when it got to the house we found the Conservative party unable to contain its desire to destroy public broadcasting in Canada, and for this purpose it was prepared to embark on a filibuster, day after interminable day, as though hon. members were determined to outdo their efforts during the flag fiasco.
I am attempting to talk in a reasonable way about an aspect of public broadcasting that I enjoy, namely radio. I am being enticed to depart from that subject by some friends of mine who sit very close to me. I intend to resist that temptation, however, and simply say that if we had more speeches of the type and quality of the speech about public broadcasting just made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South, a person who has obviously had a new view about broadcasting in recent times, we would get more of what people expect from parliament, namely a reasoned and balanced conversation about public policy. As it is, we find one particular party hell bent to destroy public broadcasting, to which end it is prepared to embark on a continuing program of vituperation which encourages among the general public a lack of perspective when it comes to the broad concept upon which the C.B.C. was founded. I have no further comment to make, other than that.
March 14, 1968

I intend to speak very briefly on this subject. I believe it is a happy coincidence that the Secretary of State should have within her jurisdiction not only the C.B.C., for which she reports to this house, but also the national arts centre currently under construction in Ottawa. I say it is a happy coincidence, because over the years the C.B.C. has had a mandate to encourage Canadian talent in the performing arts. I believe everybody in this house and in Canada generally recognizes that the C.B.C. has done an outstanding job in encouraging the performing arts in Canada. I repeat myself when I say it is a happy coincidence that the Secretary of State has the responsibility for reporting both the C.B.C. and the national arts centre. As I understand it, the new national arts centre will have a general mandate to encourage the performing arts in Canada, and I trust that the C.B.C. will co-operate to the greatest possible extent with the centre in carrying out that mandate.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I have already talked to the minister about the type of musical bodies that the arts centre will encourage initially in Ottawa. In years gone by the C.B.C., especially through its radio section, did a fine job in encouraging musical groups, although such may not necessarily be the case today.
I have also discussed this matter with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The national capitals of many countries have developed magnificent symphony orchestras, with the assistance of public funds. I do not for a minute suggest that Ottawa is a world capital in the sense that Amsterdam, Copenhagen, and some other capitals are, but I think we should make a start now by encouraging the role which the government must play in assisting the performing arts, and by urging the C.B.C. to co-operate with the new centre.
I wish publicly to thank the minister for the opportunities I have had to discuss this matter with her. I hope whoever occupies her position in the future-and I trust it will be the hon. lady herself, because she has done a good job in this respect-will encourage cooperation between the C.B.C. and the national arts centre in Ottawa.

Mr. Chairman, I think that liberties are being taken, that the standing orders are being disregarded when we deal with matters somewhat outside the scope of the subject under discussion. At this point, I
Supply-C.B.C.
should like to avail myself of the same latitude in order to express to the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) my satisfaction, and that of many Canadians, who were happy to learn today about the appointment of Hon. Georges-Emile Lapalme as chairman of an organization entrusted with the administration of an amount of approximately $10 million for film distribution.
Mr. Chairman, I think I may take the liberty of making a rather special comment, since I have known the appointee to this new position perhaps more intimately than most members, and I can say that he is a Canadian of unusual honesty, competence and loyalty. He has been noted for many years for his unfailing judgment in the field of arts, humanities, science and literature.
Hear, hear.

I wish to congratulate the hon. Secretary of State for this choice, which lead us to hope this new organization will know numerous years of fruitful accomplishments across Canada. She could not have made a better choice. Indeed, she is an old hand at it. I have already told her so, but she was not in the house at the time.
I do not say this only as a matter of courtesy which a gentleman always owes to a lady. It is in the light of results and facts. For instance, when she had the courage to say there was something rotten in the C.B.C., the Secretary of State won the admiration and the esteem of the large majority of members.
It happens that the hon. Secretary of State, in addition to her other qualities, is a Liberal. I imagine that if she were a Conservative, the same could be said about her, that is, she would have accomplished fully as much. But someone had to say some day that there was something wrong with the C.B.C. and that reform was urgently needed so that this corporation should really become the instrument of culture, national unity and common sense which it is supposed to be according to the idea of those who set it up.
I wanted to pay this tribute, Mr. Chairman, first of all in the name of all those who, like me, were concerned about certain bad habits which the C.B.C. had acquired, and who are happy to see that an effort is being made, at least, to bring about reforms and to prevent the abuses of the past.
I take personal pleasure in congratulating Mr. Lapalme for his appointment, for I had the opportunity to know him better than several of my colleagues. But I know that I
March 14, 1968

Supply-Secretary of State am expressing the feelings of many Canadians, especially those in the province of Quebec, when I say how glad we are to see that hon. Georges-Emile Lapalme has been appointed as chairman of the organization I mentioned earlier.
How long does the minister anticipate it will be before the B.B.G. is wound up and the new commission is appointed?
I think the order in council has already been passed indicating that the act will be proclaimed on April 1.

SECRETARY OF STATE A-Departmentlc. Departmental Administration, including grants as detailed in the Estimates-To extend the purposes of Secretary of State Vote 1 of the Main Estimates for 1967-68 to provide that the Centennial Commission shall cease to exist on the 1st day of April, 1968; that all rights and property held by or in the name of or in trust for the Commission, and all obligations and liabilities of the Commission, existing before that day, shall continue as the rights, property, obligations and liabilities of Her Majesty in right of Canada; and to authorize the Secretary of State to do and perform all acts and things necessary for or incidental to closing out the affairs of the Commission and to provide a further amount of, $274,400.

This is a quite considerable item and it gives me an opportunity to congratulate the minister on the work that was done during centennial year. Governments move slowly, and here I can think of the National Arts Centre which has been abuild-ing for years. Had the Secretary of State been able to find people like John Fisher, and some of the others in the Expo organization, much of the red tape could have been avoided. They were able to get the Expo operation developed in good time for centennial year.
Although there was considerable duplication of costs, I think all Canadians will look back on centennial year as a great success and something to remember with a great deal of pride. Building nationhood is a difficult process. It is often developed most during periods when a country has to make an extreme sacrifice. Canada took a great step toward nationhood each time it became engaged in a war, but I think Canadians combined together during centennial year to take a great stride forward into nationhood, thanks largely to the centennial commission's efforts.

[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I should like to congratulate that great Canadian, John Fisher, who under extreme difficulty headed up the commission and carried on even in the face of the political backbiting which went on among his friends and colleagues in the commission. He was able always to put forward the idea that it is great to be a Canadian and that one should be proud to be in Canada. I believe that his spirit as well as the utterances he made as he travelled across this country in centennial year and in preceding years, combined with the roughshod way in which the minister on many occasions administered the operation of the centennial commission and tore through the red tape, together with her ability to get things done, made it possible for all Canadians to enjoy a very fine year. Now when we are in the process of paying the bill for centennial year I think we should look back with great pride at the operation of the centennial commission. I believe this will be a memorial to the effectiveness of one woman in cabinet.

Mr. Chairman, I rise very briefly to support the remarks made by the hon. member for Timiskaming and to congratulate the minister for the role she played in our centennial year. I also congratulate her on her ability to find men during that year. I have heard it said that she was the ideal personality to fulfil the role of Secretary of State during our centennial year. She combined in her personality that duality of the traditional and the go-go.
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. After what I have heard here tonight I venture to say that the Secretary of State should run for the leadership post that is available.

Item agreed to.
2c. Construction or Acquisition of Buildings, Works, Land and Equipment-National Arts Centre, $7,500,000.

Mr. Chairman, I am very disgusted when I look at this particular project and think of the time involved in its construction. If Campeau has been able to build four or five high rise buildings in the time it takes us to put a pile of cement in a hole which has been there for three years off and on, I think it is about time we reconsidered the construction methods we use. When I went to Expo I was very impressed when I heard Mr. Shaw and others who were responsible for the development of Expo talk about
March 14, 1968

the critical path of building. The critical path of building has been a nightmare so far as the National Arts Centre is concerned. I realize that the Secretary of State probably has had nothing to do with the construction, since this no doubt comes under the Department of Public Works.
I should like to raise the point that the government service apparently has been able to obtain the knowhow in respect of the critical path of building. I would suggest that perhaps this ability in the critical path of building might be applied to the work undertaken by the Department of Public Works. If that department is not able to meet satisfactory schedules, then perhaps they should forget about building and let Campeau do it. Before the minister leaves, whether it be this year, next year or five years from now, I am sure she would like to be able to open the National Arts Centre. I am afraid that even if she is still in the department five years from now she cannot be sure that she will have this opportunity.
I believe the construction of this building is a national disgrace. The construction site is in the centre of the national capital where anyone can see it every day. We have established that we have the ability to find and hire the right people. The minister has been able to do this in respect of the very ingenious engineering projects which took place at Expo. Surely this ability can be applied to other government departments. I suggest that when the ministers obtain approval from parliament for expenditures, that they consider the critical path of construction so that when a building is to be built it will be built within a reasonable length of time. I believe that when it takes three years to construct the cement part of a building, that is too long a period. I suggest that this situation really is not satisfactory to the minister. I believe we should be very proud of the ability she has exhibited and I think that what has been accomplished in respect of the Expo construction should be extended to other works.

maintopic: INCOME TAX-PROPOSED EXEMPTION OF GUARANTEED OLD AGE INCOME SUPPLEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, March 4, as recorded in Hansard at page 7231, I put this question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare:
In view of the fact that old age pensioners between the ages of 67 and 70 who are drawing the guaranteed income supplement, even though they have no other income, are being required to pay income tax on a portion of their supplement, will the minister take up with his colleague the Minister of Finance the possibility of exempting the supplement from income tax?
The minister replied as follows:
I will be glad to discuss the matter with the Minister of Finance.
I then responded with this question:
May I expect an answer at ten o'clock one of these nights?
I can use less than my allotted seven minutes in putting this question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare tonight, in view of the fact that at 8.40 or 8.45 this evening when we were discussing the income tax bill before the house at that time I put the question to the Minister of Finance. I have to admit that the answer I got from him was not very satisfactory, so I am back where I was on Monday, March 4, urging the Minister of National Health and Welfare to make his representations to the Minister of Finance with respect to this matter.

After all, it was the Minister of National Health and Welfare who brought in the legislation providing for the guaranteed income supplement, and the point that he made over and over again was that the purpose of this legislation was to guarantee to our old age pensioners a certain minimum level of income. That minimum level was to be $105 a month for a single person, or $1,260 a year. However, as I pointed out when I was speaking during the committee stage of the debate on the income tax bill, because of the fact that a single person has a tax exemption of only $1,100, the $1,260 that he receives puts him into the income tax bracket to the point that he has to pay something over $20 a year in income tax. In the case of a married couple, the tax they would have to pay is something over $50.
In all these cases I am referring to individuals between the ages of 67 and 70. Once they are over 70, they have the extra $500 exemption and the problem disappears, at least for people at these income levels. The minister knows very well-and I am sure he will not argue with this and will not wish to misrepresent me on it-that because I believe in no means test on the old age pension, I agree that the old age security, means test-free pension has to be taxable income. That is one of the reasons that you have no means test, because you make the adjustment by means of the income tax.
So what I am talking about is not the means test-free pension but the supplement which people receive only when they are submitted to what the minister euphemistically calls an income test. Some of the rest of us still call it a means test. My point is that when persons have been submitted to a test in order to get money to bring them up to a certain level, they should not have that amount of money reduced. It is a very simple situation. The Minister of National Health and Welfare says to all his pensioner friends across the country: I have brought your income up to a certain minimum level. Then his colleague the Minister of Finance turns around and takes some of it away. I therefore ask, Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of National Health and Welfare will make strong representations to the Minister of Finance to correct this most unfortunate situation?

and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) anticipated the results of that discussion by putting the question directly to the Minister of Finance who is responsible, basically, for the income tax law. The minister put the answer on the record tonight and there is no necessity for me to repeat it.
Of course I disagree with my hon. friend when he says that there is a means test on the new guaranteed income supplement. I imagine that no matter how long we are in the house, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will continue to regard this test as a means test, while I correctly describe it as an income test. My hon. friend realizes that while this group of people to which he refers is eligible for payment of income tax, they pay this tax because they have been raised to a level of income at which all taxpayers are eligible to pay tax.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
So that what the hon. member is arguing is that in this particular case we should make a special provision which would place this group of taxpayers in a special category different from other taxpayers. The Minister of Finance has given the answer, and I have nothing to add to it.

PUBLIC SERVICE-POSITION OF EXECUTIVE AND PROFESSIONAL OFFICERS RESPECTING COLLECTIVE BARGAINING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for a period of weeks I have been endeavouring, both publicly and privately but without success, to induce the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson) to clarify the statement of government policy on the obligations in respect of collective bargaining of public servants employed in a managerial or confidential capacity, and as well to arrange the withdrawal or reversal of erroneous directives on the subject issued in certain departments. Two simple questions, proper answers to which would have clarified the situation completely, were placed on the order paper by me as numbers 1073 and 1074 as long ago as February 19, but they have been ignored completely, despite the fact that I have emphasized their urgency twice to the President of the Treasury Board and twice to his parliamentary secretary.
When no answers were forthcoming yesterday after the questions had been called seven

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion times, I was given no option but to ask this further question, which appears at page 7585 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the President of the Treasury Board whether the government has taken any action to remove misunderstandings existing in several departments of government due to erroneous directives that employees in executive or professional roles are required to resign from employee organizations before collective bargaining begins.
The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, we looked into this question which my hon. friend has raised before, and found that in one department there was an erroneous interpretation of the directive of the Treasury Board. We have been in touch with this and other departments to make sure the directive issued by the Treasury Board is adhered to within the departments.
Regrettably that answer is not correct. There was more than one department which issued an erroneous directive, and in fact no effective action has been taken to make sure the law passed by this parliament is obeyed. The result has been that a great many public servants, under a totally erroneous impression of the law, have felt compelled to resign from employee organizations, to their great personal detriment as well as to the loss of such organizations. In my view, these unrepudiated directives constitute an unfair labour practice, and I hope the record may be set completely straight tonight.
What is the law? Under the Public Service Staff Relations Act certain persons employed in a managerial or confidential capacity are placed under certain natural inhibitions with respect to collective bargaining. Obviously a managerial person cannot be both manager for the employer and negotiator for fellow employees. Conflict of interest must be avoided.
Three things are equally apparent. First, not all executive or professional employees are managerial or confidential employees who will be involved in collective bargaining, and the act does not so contemplate.
Second, the final determination of who is a managerial or confidential employee involved in the duties set out in section 2(u) of the act is vested in the public service staff relations board. It is not a unilateral determination by the employer.
Third, the act contains no prohibition of a managerial or confidential employee so determined belonging to an employee organization, provided they are in a non-voting, non-policy making, non-negotiating capacity.
7S60	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
Consequently, the employee organizations have established associate member categories to accommodate such managerial or confidential employees. These members have no right to join in decision making, but they can enjoy insurance benefits, social advantages, grievance procedure representation, and other proper benefits. Indeed, this is the only way they can enjoy the full advantages of the grievance procedure.
Earlier this year the cabinet authorized a document entitled "Statement of Government Policy on the Obligations of Public Servants Identified as Persons Employed in a Managerial or Confidential Capacity". This statement, a copy of which was laid on the table yesterday at my request as sessional paper 159E, is, in my opinion vague and ambiguous, and in its concluding paragraph, misleading, particularly in implying that it is solely the opinion of the employer which determines who is a person employed in a managerial or confidential capacity. That is for the staff relations board.
Subsequently, several departments misinterpreted the cabinet's statement of policy and issued firm and absolute directives to all managerial or confidential employees that they must separate from staff associations. I wish to quote only two. In the unemployment insurance commission, the directive dated February 15 stated:
This means that if you hold a membership in an employee organization you must terminate such membership.
The directive in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development contained this phrase:
You will lose this insurance by dissociating yourself from an employee organization, which you must now do.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, "which you must now do". This was addressed on February 22 to "all managerial and confidential exclusions".
I am told that there are several other equally erroneous directives, Mr. Speaker, and that the result has been a great many totally unnecessary resignations from some employee organizations, with consequent forfeiture of genuine benefits to executive and professional employees, some of them of long standing. I consider this, sir, to be unfair, discriminatory and intimidating labour practices, as they are defined under the provisions of section 9 of the act.

DEBATES	March 14, 1968
In my respectful submission the cabinet statement of policy should be revised and stripped of its ambiguities and improper influences. The improper and erroneous departmental directives should be withdrawn, and all employees to whom they were sent should be advised of their withdrawal. I ask the government to make clear the undoubted fact that the type of associate membership set up, for example, by the Professional Institute and the Public Service Alliance for managerial and confidential employees is wholly unobjectionable, and indeed that such employees should in fact be encouraged to enjoy the undoubted benefits of such associate membership.

maintopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS-REDUCTION IN BUDGET FOR NORTHERN HEALTH SERVICES
NORTHERN AFFAIRS-REDUCTION IN BUDGET FOR NORTHERN HEALTH SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again as a result of the directives which have been issued by the Department of National Health and Welfare I think we have created in Canada another barrier between the Indian people and the government of Canada in its efforts to bring these people into the mainstream of Canadian life. Today I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare whether he was prepared to refer to the committee on health and welfare the question of medical services to the Indian people. Part of his reply I found most satisfactory, as it had an effect on the Northwest Territories and the northern health service situation. He told me then that he would undertake a personal, detailed review of the situation. He said that until he had concluded that review he could not prejudge the question of placing the matter before a parliamentary committee.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
Here I think we face an ideological dispute, or some misunderstanding. It is my impression that the philosophy of the Department of National Health and Welfare has been that the health of Canadian Indians is not the responsibility of the federal government. In my hand I have treaty No. 11. If you examine that treaty, which was signed by the Indian people of northern Canada, you will find nothing about health services. However, in the report of the commissioner, H. A. Conroy, which is dated October 12, 1921, we find this paragraph:
Practically all the bands dealt with wanted more provision for medical attendance at each post, schools for their children, and supplies for their old and destitute.
I pointed out that they were still able to make their own living, and that Dr. A. L. McDonald, of the Indian department, was then with me, and that they could see him, and that he would attend them free if they wished, but that it was impossible for the government to furnish regular
DEBATES	7661
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
medical attention, when they were occupying such a vast tract of territory.
Regardless of whether the government of Canada is legally responsible to the Indian people of Canada for medical health services, I believe it has a moral, ethical and traditional responsibility. I do not suggest that the Indian people of Canada will not soon look after their own medical services; I suggest that the directive which was issued by the government in the Manitoba zone on March 6 does not add up, when it says:
The bands should establish health committees whose duty it would be "to determine what Indians of the band are medically indigent". These committees should meet at regular intervals in order to keep their records of indigents up to date.
Also in the same directive it says:
Indian bands that have funds must make their own arrangements for the purchase of treatment services either by paying local physicians directly or by arranging to take part in medical insurance programs. If Indian bands wish to purchase insured medical services, whereby Indian people can go to any doctor of their choosing, medical services branch will consider assisting such bands in the payment of such insured services.
I have read many documents issued by many government departments but never have I read one more ambiguous. The effects of this document may lead to a deterioration in relations which have been so carefully built up. Through the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and through community development programs we have tried to bring the Indians of Canada into the mainstream of Canadian life. Yet we have here an example of one government department doing something contrary to the policy of another. I do not know whether there was liaison, but certainly there was no advance warning that this directive to cut down services would be issued. Certainly there was no consultation in this matter with Indian advisers and councillors.
Here we have a directive coming from an agency of government which, so far as I am concerned, may destroy the relationships which we have tried to build up in this country. I know the Minister of National Health and Welfare is deeply concerned about the matter and I know he feels strongly about it. I ask him to re-examine the situation, and if there are to be changes, to let those changes be known long before they are to take place. But, in the name of heaven, let us not further destroy the confidence that the Indian people of Canada have in their government.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS-REDUCTION IN BUDGET FOR NORTHERN HEALTH SERVICES
speechtext:
The question which the hon. member for Northwest Territories asked is very complicated and it is impossible to deal with it adequately in a few minutes.
Of course the main objective of our service, so far as the Indian population is concerned, is to make sure that our Indians belong to the mainstream of the Canadian community. The best way to ensure that any person in the Canadian community is in the mainstream is to ensure that dependency is reduced and independence established. This will certainly be the objective for all groups in Canada, including the Indian population. In the Department of National Health and Welfare we have been obliged, as have other departments, to scrutinize our estimated expenditures for the coming year, and while we have been able to maintain at least the same level of expenditures for northern health services and Indian health services as was established last year, we have not been able to maintain the significant increase which prevailed over the preceding year; we increased the level of expenditures in northern health services in that year over the former year by about 14 per cent.
Given a definite budget, the officers of the medical service have had to accommodate the service provided within those budgetary

limits. Certainly the members of the department are sympathetic to the needs of the Indian population, and of the population of northern Canada. This interest and sympathy has been expressed by the continuing efforts to improve the level of services. But we have been obliged to readjust, rearrange and in some cases to curtail services for the coming year.
I have listened with great interest to the representations of the hon. member for the Northwest Territories and to other representations which have been made, and I am currently reviewing the situation in an effort to ensure that minimum changes are made in this service. There is no lack of sympathy or concern. The consideration is a budgetary one in relation to other demands on the curtailed estimates of the department. I shall be discussing this problem with my colleagues and I hope that at the end of this discussion and review I shall be able to make a more definite statement about these services.
